text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Friedlander v. Claman,

2015 BCSC 482

Date: 20150330

Docket:
E132630

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Eran
Chaim Friedlander

Claimant

And

Jody
Lynne Claman and 567773 BC Ltd. (Inc. No. 567773)

Respondents

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Gropper

Reasons for Judgment on Costs

Counsel for the Claimant:

K.
Thompson

Counsel for the Respondents:

S.
El-Khatib

Written Submissions of the Claimant:

January
15, and

February 12, 2015

Written Submissions of the Respondents:

February
5, 2015

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

March
30, 2015

I.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The claimant in this family law case, Mr. Friedlander,
brings an application on costs in regard to my reasons for judgment released on
August 7, 2014 (“August Reasons”), and November 17, 2014 (“November Reasons”).
The orders, substantially in Mr. Friedlander’s favour, were settled on
December 19, 2014. I directed that I would receive written submissions on
costs.

[
2
]

Mr. Friedlander seeks an order for special costs
of the entirety of these proceedings under Rule 16-1(1) of the
Supreme Court
Family Rules
, B.C. Reg. 169/2009 [
Family

Rules
] on the basis
of the alleged reprehensible conduct of the respondent, Ms. Claman, which,
Mr. Friedlander submits, is deserving of reproof or rebuke.

[
3
]

Alternatively, Mr. Friedlander seeks costs
of these proceedings up to November 14, 2014, and double costs under Rule
11-1(5), for all steps taken thereafter on the basis that the final order in
this proceeding was substantially more favourable to him when compared to an
offer of settlement made by him to Ms. Claman on November 14, 2013.

[
4
]

As a further alternative, Mr. Friedlander submits
that these proceedings were of more than ordinary difficulty, pursuant to s. 1(1)
of Appendix B of the
Family

Rules
, and, therefore, seeks that
costs, pursuant to Rule 16-1, be assessed accordingly.

[
5
]

Ms. Claman’s position is that an award of
special costs is not appropriate since special costs are an extraordinary
remedy and her conduct, as well as the circumstances of the parties, does not
justify such an award. She further submits that double costs should not be
ordered.

II.

Background

[
6
]

The parties began living together in November
2006 and were married on August 21, 2007, one month before their daughter was
born.

[
7
]

They separated on September 10, 2013.

[
8
]

The notice of family claim was filed by Mr. Friedlander
on September 12, 2013. Ms. Claman filed a response of October 25, 2013,
and a counterclaim on March 31, 2014. Mr. Friedlander responded to the
counterclaim on May 6, 2014.

[
9
]

The parties attended a judicial case conference
before Mr. Justice Pearlman on October 17, 2013. Consent orders were made that
each party refrain from making disparaging comments about the other in their
daughter’s presence and that Ms. Claman deliver her Form F8 financial
statement and response to family claim to Mr. Friedlander’s counsel on or
before October 25, 2013.

[
10
]

On November 6 and 22, 2013, Master Scarth heard
Mr. Friedlander’s application pertaining to increased and specified
parenting time with their daughter and made interim orders regarding shared
custody and guardianship, equal parenting time and other parenting details, as
well as an order for a s. 211 report. The parties were mutually restrained
from attending at or near the other party’s residence or place of work and
restrained from making false and defamatory statements to or about the other
party in public.

[
11
]

The parties were before Master Scarth again on
December 17, 2013. She dismissed Ms. Claman’s application for short leave
to vary the November 22, 2013 order and, by consent, ordered that Ms. Claman’s
application for a restraining order by adjourned. She extended the deadline by
which Ms. Claman must produce documents requested by Mr. Friedlander’s
counsel until February 1, 2014.

[
12
]

In my November Reasons, indexed as
2014 BCSC
2136
, I described the events pertaining to disclosure which took place after
Master Scarth’s December 2013 order:

[11] On December 17, 2013, Master Scarth
ordered Ms. Claman’s documents be produced on or before February 1, 2014.

[12] There was continuing correspondence
between counsel (initiated for the most part by Mr. Friedlander’s counsel) and
Ms. Claman’s counsel (who changed several times) about disclosure.
Disclosure was not made in accordance with the court orders or requests by
claimant’s counsel.

[13] In March 2014, counsel for both parties
signed a joint retainer letter appointing Vern Blair of Blair Mackay Mynett
Valuations Inc. to value the parties’ corporate interests.

[14] An examination for discovery of
Ms. Claman was conducted on May 8, 2014. Mr. Friedlander’s counsel
made numerous requests for documents, which gave rise to a short leave application
for production of documents before Master McNaughton on May 30, 2014. Some, but
not all of the documents were provided before the trial commenced.

[15] Master McNaughton made a further order
on May 30, 2014 in respect of financial documentation including documents
relating to any loans to Ms. Claman, bank statements of the businesses,
general ledgers of the businesses, cheques, bank statements, mortgage
documentation, and corporate tax returns. She was also required to produce
documents in the possession of her accountant, Brian McKay of any shareholders
agreements, trust agreements, minute books, shareholding ledgers and any other
document referring to her interest in Glass House Holdings.

[16] Ms. Claman did not comply with her
obligation to produce documents nor did she comply with court orders to do so.

[17] Despite the
fact that the parties jointly retained Blair Mackay Mynett Valuations Inc. to
prepare estimates as to the fair market value of all the issued and outstanding
shares of Glass House Holdings Ltd., Jody’s Fine Foods Inc. and 567773 B.C.
Ltd., Ms. Claman failed to provide the necessary documentation to enable
that valuation to proceed in respect of her business interests. As such, the
value of Ms. Claman’s corporate holdings is unknown.

[
13
]

In June and July of 2014, the parties were
before me for a highly charged and publicized two week trial, following which I
provided two sets of reasons for judgment. My oral August Reasons specifically
addressed where the parties’ daughter should attend school, whether Mr. Friedlander
should have final decision-making authority in respect of the child’s education
and her cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage and
whether the child should have a cell phone. My November Reasons dealt with the
remaining issues of division of family assets and debts, child support and
spousal support.

[
14
]

In the midst of trial, I made an order on June
23, 2014, that nothing from the trial be tweeted by any party, particularly Ms. Claman,
and that anything on social media about the trial be removed from all social
networks. In the final order on August 7, 2014, this was worded as follows:
“Neither the claimant nor the respondent may post anything about the trial,
these proceedings or [their daughter] on any form of social media, including,
without limiting the foregoing, Twitter, Facebook and LinkedIn.”

[
15
]

At the conclusion of the trial I ordered,
inter
alia
, the following:

•

joint custody and shared guardianship, as well
as equal parenting time, are in the best interests of the parties’ daughter;

•

Mr. Friedlander is to have final decision-making
authority in respect of their daughter’s education and cultural, linguistic,
religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage;

•

the parties’ daughter is to continue attending
Vancouver Talmud Torah until the end of grade 7, as sought by Mr. Friedlander;

•

neither parent is to give or permit their
daughter to have a cell phone with the other parent’s written authorization, as
sought by Mr. Friedlander;

•

in order to equalize the division of net family
assets, Ms. Claman (or the corporate respondents in her name) is to pay
Mr. Friedlander the sum of $593,893.31 by January 15, 2015;

•

Ms. Claman is imputed an annual guideline income
of $200,000 for child support purposes, therefore, neither party shall pay
basic child support to the other;

•

Ms. Claman is to pay Mr. Friedlander the
sum of $9,800 for her equal share of the special or extraordinary expenses
incurred by him; and

•

Ms. Claman’s claim for spousal support is
dismissed.

[
16
]

Mr. Friedlander was entirely successful in these
proceedings.

[
17
]

On November 18, 2014, Ms. Claman began the
appeal process. On December 24, 2014, she filed an application asking, among
other things, that my order requiring her to pay Mr. Friedlander the
equalization payment on or before January 15, 2015, be stayed pending the
disposition of her appeal to the B.C. Court of Appeal. She further filed a
short-leave application on January 26, 2015, asking that the certificates of
pending litigation (“CPLs”) on three of her properties be released so that she
could mortgage the properties in order to comply with the equalization payment order.

[
18
]

Upon the hearing of these two applications on
January 29, 2015, I ordered that no party be permitted to bring short leave
applications before any judge or master besides myself, that I be seized of all
matters in these proceedings, that the CPLs remain in place, that Ms. Claman
be permitted to mortgage the three properties in the total sum of $855,000 with
provisions and that Ms. Claman’s application for a stay of proceedings be
dismissed.

III.

Special Costs

A.

Legal Framework

[
19
]

The courts hold both legislative authority and
inherent jurisdiction to award costs. In the family law context, Rule 16-1(7) of
the
Family Rules
codifies the traditional rule that costs follow the
event stating that, subject to subrule (9), costs of a family law case must be
awarded to the successful party unless the court otherwise orders. The policies
that underpin this approach were discussed by the Supreme Court of Canada in
British Columbia (Minister of Forests) v. Okanagan Indian Band
,
2003 SCC 71 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 371 at para.
26
:

Indeed, the
traditional approach to costs can also be viewed as being animated by the broad
concern to ensure that the justice system works fairly and efficiently. Because
costs awards transfer some of the winner's litigation expenses to the loser
rather than leaving each party's expenses where they fall (as is done in
jurisdictions without costs rules), they act as a disincentive to those who
might be tempted to harass others with meritless claims. And because they
offset to some extent the outlays incurred by the winner, they make the legal
system more accessible to litigants who seek to vindicate a legally sound
position. These effects of the traditional rules can be connected to the
court's concern with overseeing its own process and ensuring that litigation is
conducted in an efficient and just manner. In this sense it is a natural
evolution in the law to recognize the related policy objectives that are served
by the modern approach to costs.

[
20
]

Rule 16-1(1) dictates that the assessment of
costs occurs in accordance with Appendix B of the
Family Rules
unless
certain circumstances exist. Subrule (4) further guides that disbursements must
have been necessarily or properly incurred in the conduct of the family law
case and must be of a reasonable amount. Recently in
Gichuru v. Smith
,

2014 BCCA 414
at para.
106
, the Court of Appeal reasoned that, although a
judge has the discretion to determine the quantum of costs, it is a discretion
to be exercised sparingly since the “court officer best placed to determine if
the fees billed by a lawyer are objectively reasonable is usually the
registrar.”

[
21
]

A special costs award departs from the traditional
approach to the award and assessment of costs.

[
22
]

I considered the law of special costs in
Westsea
Construction Ltd. v. 0759553 B.C. Ltd.
,
2013 BCSC 1352
at paras.
27 -
37
, where I stated, in part:

[28]

The leading authority for special costs in British Columbia is the
Court of Appeal’s decision
Garcia v. Crestbrook Forest Industries Ltd
.
(1994),
1994 CanLII 2570 (BC CA)
, 9 B.C.L.R. (3d) 242 (C.A.). There, Mr. Justice Lambert, writing for the
court, determined that the threshold for awarding special costs is
“reprehensible” conduct.

…

[30]

In the decision on special costs, Lambert J.A. noted that different
terms had been used to describe the appropriate circumstances for awarding
special costs. In particular, he drew attention to the finding of Madam Justice
McLachlin (as she then was) in the Supreme Court of Canada decision
Young v.
Young
,
1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
, [1993] 4 S.C.R. 3 in regard to costs (with which the majority
concurred) at 134:

Solicitor-client
costs are generally awarded only where there has been reprehensible, scandalous
or outrageous conduct on the part of one of the parties.

[31]

Lambert J.A. reviewed other decisions as well. He noted the
discussion in
Leung v. Leung

(1993), 77 B.C.L.R. (2d) 314 (S.C.) at
para. 5
, where Chief Justice Esson (as he then was) observed that the term
“reprehensible” was of wide meaning, capturing both scandalous and outrageous
conduct as well as milder forms of misconduct deserving of rebuke. He also
considered
Fullerton v. Matsqui (District)
(1992),
1992 CanLII 5985 (BC CA)
, 74 B.C.L.R. (2d) 305
(C.A.) at 309, which applied the standard of “misbehaviour in the conduct of
this litigation” that made the award of special costs a “desirable ... form of
chastisement”.

[32]

Lambert J.A. decided to introduce clarity into the law of special
costs by synthesizing the different variations on the standard for a special
costs award into a single standard, that of reprehensible conduct. He held at
para. 17:

Having regard to
the terminology adopted by Madam Justice McLachlin
in
Young v. Young
, to
the terminology adopted by Mr. Justice Cumming
in
Fullerton v. Matsqui
(District)
, and to the application of the standard of "reprehensible
conduct" by Chief Justice Esson in
Leung v. Leung
in awarding
special costs in circumstances where he had explicitly found that the conduct
in question was neither scandalous nor outrageous, but could only be
categorized as one of the "milder forms of misconduct" which could
simply be said to be "deserving of reproof or rebuke",
it is my
opinion that the single standard for the awarding of special costs is that the
conduct in question properly be categorized as "reprehensible"
.
As Chief Justice Esson said in
Leung v. Leung
, the word reprehensible is
a word of wide meaning. It encompasses scandalous or outrageous conduct but it
also encompasses milder forms of misconduct deserving of reproof or rebuke.
Accordingly, the standard represented by the word reprehensible, taken in that
sense, must represent a general and all-encompassing expression of the
applicable standard for the award of special costs.

[Emphasis added.]

[33]

Lambert J.A. recognized that the meaning of “reprehensible” conduct
was still quite broad. In order for a special costs award to be justified, the
circumstances had to be exceptional. He continued at paras. 23 and 25:

However, the fact
that an action or an appeal "has little merit" is not in itself a
reason for awarding special costs. ...
Something more is required
, such
as improper allegations of fraud, or an improper motive for bringing the
proceedings, or improper conduct of the proceedings themselves, before the
conduct becomes sufficiently reprehensible to require an award of special costs.

...

If the proceedings
are taken, not in the reasonable expectation of a satisfactory outcome, but in
order to impose the burden of the proceedings themselves on the opposing party
in circumstances where one party is financially much stronger than the other,
then the absence of merit, coupled with the improper motive, is in my opinion a
combination which may well amount to reprehensible conduct sufficient to
require an award of special costs.

[Emphasis added in

Westsea
.]

…

[37]

More importantly,
Garcia
emphasizes that the purpose of a
special costs award is to chastise a litigant. By rebuking reprehensible
conduct, the court punishes bad behaviour and deters it. It also serves to
distance the court from the conduct at issue.

[
23
]

In
Tomic v. Tough
,
2013 BCCA 355
at para.
35
,
our Court of Appeal confirmed that the test for a special costs award as set
out in
Garcia
applies in the family law context.

[
24
]

I went on to say at para. 38 of
Westsea

that despite Lambert J.A.’s effort to clearly articulate the threshold for
awarding special costs in
Garcia
, it can be difficult to apply this
standard because the concept of “reprehensibility” captures a wide range of
misconduct, special costs awards are determined on a case by case basis, and it
is sometimes challenging to pinpoint the outer limits of what is reprehensible.
What is key to the analysis is the exceptional element or “something more”. I
agree that the application of special costs should be limited to exceptional
circumstances. The Supreme Court of Canada very recently affirmed this
“exceptional” circumstances threshold at para. 137 of
Carter v. Canada
(Attorney General)
,
2015 SCC 5
, when clarifying the test for special costs
in cases involving public interest litigants.

[
25
]

In
Westsea
, I reviewed the jurisprudence
in the following thematic groups: meritless claims and improper motive (paras. 42
- 52); abuse of the court’s process (paras. 53 - 57); sharp practice
derogating from the rules of professional conduct and the rules of court
(paras. 58 - 64); and misleading the court (paras. 65 - 72). I
proceeded in this way not to impose a categorical approach upon special costs
awards, but to provide a guide when faced with similar factual circumstances.

[
26
]

I summarized my findings at para. 73 by
providing principles for awarding special costs:

[73]

I have undertaken a thorough review of the cases involving special
costs. Having examined the authorities provided by both sides, it is apparent
to me that the courts have been somewhat inconsistent in their determination of
what amounts to reprehensible conduct and that those authorities must be
reconciled. Based upon my review of the authorities, I have derived the
following principles for awarding special costs:

a)

the court must exercise restraint in awarding specials costs;

b)

the party seeking special costs must demonstrate exceptional
circumstances to justify a special costs order;

c)

simply because the legal concept of “reprehensibility” captures
different kinds of misconduct does not mean that all forms of misconduct are
encompassed by this term;

d)

reprehensibility will likely be found in circumstances where there
is evidence of improper motive, abuse of the court’s process, misleading the
court and persistent breaches of the rules of professional conduct and the
rules of court that prejudice the applicant;

e)

special costs can be ordered against parties and non-parties alike;
and

f)

the
successful litigant is entitled to costs in accordance with the general rule
that costs follow the event. Special costs are not awarded to a successful
party as a “bonus” or further compensation for that success.

B.

Positions of the Parties

[
27
]

Mr. Friedlander submits that Ms. Claman has
persistently engaged in blameworthy and reprehensible conduct for which the
courts have, in other circumstances, and should, in this circumstance, award
special costs. In particular, he describes her actions based on five categories
and relies on case law for each. I will consider each category of conduct in
turn.

[
28
]

Ms. Claman submits that her conduct does not
approach the reprehensible conduct described in other cases, such as
A.S.P.
v. N.N.J.
,
2013 BCSC 2377
, in which the father “conducted himself in the
litigation as a malicious bully” (para. 12). She further asserts that even
in such cases where special costs are required, the surrounding facts are
considered in determining the quantum of special costs. Ms. Claman submits
that this case demonstrates the reality of hard-fought issues and that the relative
financial circumstances of the parties, along with significant hardship,
militate against the awarding of special costs.

C.

Is Mr. Friedlander Entitled to Special Costs?

[
29
]

I now consider each of the five categories of
conduct to which Mr. Friedlander points to justify an award for special
costs against Ms. Claman, as well as the militating factors put forward by
Ms. Claman.

1.

Attempts to Mislead or Deceive the Court

[
30
]

Mr. Friedlander relies on the following cases in
which special costs were awarded due to attempts to mislead or deceive the
court:
Kim v. Hong
,
2013 BCSC 2248
at para.
10
;
Bains v. Bains
,

2006 BCSC 1187
at paras.
19 and 20
; and
Sarkodee-Adoo v. Sarkodee-Adoo
,

2004 BCCA 105
at para.
27
. He submits that Ms. Claman continually
attempted to mislead the court, both pre, post and during the trial. He asserts
that she attempted to manipulate both the court and Dr. England, who
provided a s. 211 report in relation to their daughter.

[
31
]

Mr. Friedlander relies on my finding at para. 112
of my August Reasons, where I stated:

[112] I am
further convinced that Ms. Claman will say anything she thinks will assist her
to achieve her ends with no regard to the truth. I disagree with Dr. England
that Ms. Claman does not know the effect that she has on others. I am certain
that Ms. Claman knows the effect that she has on others. She has manipulated
the child. She has attempted to manipulate Dr. England, and I find that she has
tried to manipulate this Court.

[
32
]

He further relies on the statement at para. 27
of my November Reasons that “[t]here are several examples of Ms. Claman’s
lack of credibility and her attempts to mislead the court.”

[
33
]

In response to Mr. Friedlander’s assertion
that her evidence was untruthful and evasive, Ms. Claman points to the
Court of Appeal’s statement  in
A.B.Z v. A.L.F.A.
,
2015 BCSC 34
at para.
34
:

While the giving
of untruthful testimony has been found to be a reprehensible form of conduct
warranting an award of special costs, that does not necessarily mean that
special costs will always be awarded simply because the witness has been
untruthful:
Unternaher v. Wheat Sheaf Inn Ltd.
(1998),
1998 CanLII 6498 (BC CA)
, 114 B.C.A.C. 299
at para.
15
.

[
34
]

I considered this case at para. 70 of
Westsea
:

[70]

The Court of Appeal has cautioned that an untruthful witness will
not always attract an award of special costs. In
Unternaher v. Wheat Sheaf
Inn Ltd
. (1999),
1998 CanLII 6498 (BC CA)
, 114 B.C.A.C. 299, the court allowed the appeal of the
trial judge’s decision to decline to award special costs. The trial judge had
found that while the defendant’s employees had concocted their evidence on
issues that directly impacted the question of liability, the defendant had not
acted reprehensibly. The Court of Appeal cautioned that its decision was not to
be taken as authority for the proposition that special costs should be awarded
simply because a witness is untruthful, although in this particular case it was
merited as the testimony was designed to defeat the plaintiff’s claim. I
extract from this reasoning that there must be evidence of some improper motive
at play.

[
35
]

While a mere finding against Ms. Claman’s
credibility is not sufficient to justify special costs, a finding that Ms. Claman
deliberately attempted to deceive this Court can justify special costs. As
noted above, I found in both my August Reasons and November Reasons that Ms. Claman
did attempt to manipulate and deceive the court.

[
36
]

In my August Reasons, I stated the following at
para. 33:

Ms. Claman made
other allegations about Mr. Friedlander and his parenting abilities and
she agreed were sometimes made in the child's presence. For instance, she has
alleged that he does not look after the child properly and is incapable of
doing so. He does not support the child financially. The child goes to school
sick when she is in his care. He drives the child to school when he is drunk.
He poses a flight risk if allowed to travel internationally with the child. He
has hit the child in the face with his iPad. He told the child that Jews are
chosen people. He is a criminal. He sexually abuses the child. His father and
brother are criminals. The child is afraid of Mr. Friedlander's mother.
Mr. Friedlander's sister is a thief. Mr. Friedlander stole items from
Twin Creek belonging to Ms. Claman. She also alleged in her evidence that
Mr. Friedlander has gangland ties and does business with known gang
members.

[
37
]

After making these allegations, Ms. Claman
admitted in her closing submissions that Mr. Friedlander is an excellent
father. She also said that their daughter’s views as reported by Dr. England
should not be relied upon because she had influenced her daughter.

[
38
]

I concluded at para. 107:

I found Ms.
Claman to exaggerate, to embellish, and to avoid answering questions. Her
evidence was internally inconsistent and inconsistent with what she stated in
examination for discovery or in affidavits filed with this Court. She admitted
in her argument that much of what Mr. Friedlander said was true, although that
did not appear to be her position when she gave evidence.

[
39
]

As noted above, I found at para. 112 that
her attempts to manipulate this court and Dr. England were intentional.

[
40
]

In my November Reasons, I provided some specific
examples of Ms. Claman’s attempts to mislead the court:

[27] There are several examples of
Ms. Claman’s lack of credibility and her attempts to mislead the court.

[28] A significant example is her inflating
her assets at the commencement of the relationship and enhancing the debts at
the end of the relationship. Her obvious goal is to diminish the value of her
assets at the end of the marriage and claim for debts that are not supported by
documentation, are not properly claimed as family debts or were incurred after
separation and not for a family purpose.

[29] Throughout her evidence,
Ms. Claman said that her store, Glass House Holdings, actually belonged to
her daughter. She claimed she had no interest in the store as an owner or a
beneficial owner. In her closing submissions, she admitted that she was a
beneficial owner of Glass House Holdings, which conformed to the documentary
evidence that she is the sole director and shareholder and controls the company.
She also says, for the first time in her closing submissions that her source of
funds to support her lifestyle and pay her expenses is taken out of the bank
account of Glass House Holdings. It appears to be pre-tax dollars. The only
documents related to the value of Glass House Holdings are the financial
statements for the year end of April 30, 2013 which are in “draft for
discussion purposes only” form.

[30] Ms. Claman did not provide any
independent evidence about any of her corporate assets. She said that questions
should be directed to her accountant. She did not call her accountant as a
witness.

[31] Other examples of Ms. Claman’s
lack of credibility and attempts at misleading the court involve her stating
that Glass House Holdings was damaged in March 2013 and that the store did not
reopen. The documentary evidence shows that the store was open from time to
time and the credits before and after the damage remained the same.

[32] Ms. Claman agreed that she was
paid to be a cast member on the Real Housewives show although she diminished the
actual amount that she was paid. She did not declare it as income on her financial
statements or in her income tax return.

[33] Ms. Claman made insurance claims
in respect of the damage at Glass House Holdings but her documentation of those
claims is lacking. She also apparently claimed for losses that she did not
sustain, including a claim for staff labour costs when she had no employees.

[34] Ms. Claman claims that her property in
Whistler was damaged in January of 2013 and is inhabitable. The evidence was
that the parties stayed at that property after the alleged damage occurred. She
made insurance claims, which were paid by the insurance company. She has
provided no evidence to the contrary. The appraiser’s photographs of that
property do not show any property damage.

[35] The presence and absence of certain
assets is uncertain due to Ms. Claman’s equivocal evidence. She said she
gave the contents of a wine cellar to a friend from whom she received $50,000
for support. She lists it as one of her debts.

[36] Ms. Claman’s claim says that the
art which was present in the family home was lent to her and has been returned.
The photographs taken by the appraiser of the Twin Creek property shows that
the art that she says has been returned remains in Twin Creek.

[37] I am unable
to rely on Ms. Claman’s evidence. Where the evidence is in dispute, which
is in most cases, I must accept the evidence of Mr. Friedlander about whom
no lack of credibility has been proven.

[
41
]

Ms. Claman’s actions point to more than a mere
finding against her credibility. I find that she deliberately attempted to
mislead and deceive the court on numerous occasions and that such deception,
when viewed along with the conduct described below, justifies an award of
special costs against Ms. Claman.

2.

Disobeying a Court Order

[
42
]

Relying on the same three cases, Mr. Friedlander
submits that Ms. Claman has disobeyed and disregarded several court orders
including the court order for production of documents, the order preventing the
parties from speaking ill of the other parent in front of their daughter, the
court order prohibiting the respondent from posting anything about the trial or
the parties’ daughter on social media and the orders that she pay specific
costs.

[
43
]

Ms. Claman asserts that the court must take all
the circumstances of the case into account. She relies on
McIvor v. McIvor
,

2014 BCSC 2337
, in which the claimant refused to comply with orders and the
respondent was substantially successful, however the court ultimately did not
find special costs to be appropriate.

[
44
]

I agree with Mr. Friedlander in his reply
submissions that this situation can be distinguished from the mother’s behaviour
in
McIvor
. In that case, the mother initially refused to comply with
some of the terms of the consent order that the parties had entered into, applied
to set the order aside, was unsuccessful and, over time, took steps to comply
with the consent order. The court was not satisfied that special costs were
appropriate in that case, further citing the fact that the parties’ children
lived with their mother and such an award would present significant hardship to
the mother and children. The totality of Ms. Claman’s actions is much more
egregious than the actions of the mother in
McIvor
. I will address the
hardship issue later in my reasons.

[
45
]

As described in para. 12 above, I found in
my November Reasons that Ms. Claman deliberately and persistently did not
comply with her obligation to produce documents nor did she comply with court
orders to do so.

[
46
]

Ms. Claman has made many allegations about Mr. Friedlander
and his parenting abilities and she agreed at trial that these comments were
sometimes made in their daughter’s presence despite the court order preventing
the parties from speaking ill of the other parent in front of their daughter.

[
47
]

I will address Ms. Claman’s lack of
disclosure below. I find that while not complying with the other mentioned
court orders is a serious issue, in the circumstances of this case, this action
alone does not meet the “reprehensible” threshold. However, it is part of the
bigger picture.

3.

Using “Delay Tactics” including the Frustration
of Court Procedures

[
48
]

Again relying on
Kim
,
Bains
and
Sarkodee-Adoo
,
Mr. Friedlander submits that using delay tactics such as complying with
disclosure orders slowly and attempting to “meander, prevaricate and dissemble”
throughout trial justifies an award of special costs. He asserts that Ms. Claman
obstructed and delayed the orderly conduct of the proceedings by changing
counsel repeatedly, threatening Mr. Friedlander repeatedly, failing to
provide the business valuator (that her counsel had agreed to) with the
information necessary to provide a valuation and failing to provide disclosure.

[
49
]

Mr. Friedlander submits that Ms. Claman’s
conduct which has caused him unnecessary costs was again recently demonstrated
when she failed to agree in a timely manner to adjourn her application for a
stay to a more suitable date. Mr. Friedlander was forced to prepare
materials and have alternate counsel available to speak to an adjournment.

[
50
]

While sharp practice and delay alone may not
result in an award of special costs, I noted at para. 62 of
Westsea

that the Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge’s special costs award against
the appellants in
Grewal v. Nijjer
,
2011 BCCA 505
, finding at para.
17
:
“[t]he Nijjers put Mr. Grewal to much trouble and expense in striving to
obtain proper document discovery and particulars, only to be met with what the
judge found to be ‘ongoing delay and obfuscation’”.

[
51
]

While Ms. Claman’s delay tactics would not,
in themselves, justify an award of special costs, these actions are part of the
bigger picture of Ms. Claman’s reprehensible conduct throughout the
proceedings.

4.

Non-disclosure of Assets

[
52
]

Mr. Friedlander relies on
Kim
,
Bains
and

Sarkodee-Adoo
, as well as
Cunha v. Cunha
(1994),
1994 CanLII 3195 (BC SC)
, 99 B.C.L.R. (2d)
93, in which non-disclosure of assets was described as the “cancer” of family
litigation. He submits that Ms. Claman continually failed to disclose
documents requested pursuant to requests for documents, requests made at her
examinations for discovery and even after court orders required those documents
be produced.

[
53
]

I have described the details of this
non-disclosure above at para. 12. Because of Ms. Claman’s
non-disclosure, I was driven to draw an adverse inference against her at para. 25
of my November Reasons. I could not attribute a value to her corporate
interests at the commencement of the parties’ relationship nor at its
conclusion. This was entirely due to Ms. Claman’s failure to disclose. However,
it would have been entirely speculative to consider an increase or decrease in
the value of her assets without even sparse evidence to consider. I did,
however, have enough evidence to impute an income of $200,000 to Ms. Claman,
based upon her corporate assets.

[
54
]

Making an adverse inference in the face of
non-disclosure does not preclude an award of special costs for the same lack of
disclosure. In
Cunha
, the trial judge, at para. 42, had no
hesitation in giving Mrs. Cunha an award of special costs, “given the
completely unnecessary character of this litigation, given the persistent
obstruction and concealment on the part of Mr. Cunha.”

[
55
]

As stated by Griffin J. at para. 23 of
Kim
:

The
non-disclosure of assets has been described as the cancer of family litigation:

Cunha v. da Cunha
,
1994 CanLII 3195 (BC SC)
, [1994] B.C.J. No. 2573, at para.
9
. The remedy of
special costs in a case where there has been persistent non-disclosure is one
way of treating this cancer. …

[
56
]

Mrs. Claman’s non-disclosure was not
inadvertent; it was deliberate and persistent and is deserving of rebuke by an
award of special costs.

5.

Dissipation of Assets

[
57
]

Finally, Mr. Friedlander further relies on
Kim

and
Sarkodee-Adoo
to support that Ms. Claman’s dissipation of
family assets justifies an award of special costs.

[
58
]

He submits that Ms. Claman dissipated the
value of an asset by taking out a $100,000 mortgage against the equity in the
Twin Creek property, even though she was fully aware that he was making a claim
on that property. He further points to her inconsistent testimony related to
the contents of the wine cellar and the Bobby Burgess art.

[
59
]

These issues were addressed in my November
Reasons at paras. 52 and 53.

[
60
]

In isolation, these actions and Ms. Claman’s
inconsistent testimony about them would not be enough to be considered
“reprehensible” conduct.

[
61
]

I am satisfied, however, that the totality of
the above conduct is reprehensible and that this is an “exceptional”
circumstance which more than justifies an award of special costs.

6.

Militating Factors

[
62
]

First, Ms. Claman submits that the fact
that the issue which consumed the largest portion of trial time (the choice of
school for their daughter) was hard-fought ought to play a central role in the
determination of special costs. She asserts that her position on the issue was
supported by Dr. England in the s. 211 report.

[
63
]

As I have noted above, Ms. Claman attempted
to manipulate Dr. England during the s. 211 report preparation. I
ultimately disagreed with Dr. England’s recommendation regarding the
choice of school for the parties’ daughter, in part, because Dr. England’s
assessment of her current school was based upon Ms. Claman’s and to some extent
the child’s description of it, having been influenced by Ms. Claman.
Further, I found that Ms. Claman was not candid with Dr. England
about her main objection to the current school; she wanted to change her
daughter’s school because of the location of it, not for religious reasons.

[
64
]

Ms. Claman cannot rely on a report which I have
determined was tainted by her manipulation of its author in order to militate
against a special costs award.

[
65
]

Second, Ms. Claman submits that the trial
was unduly lengthened because Mr. Friedlander called numerous unnecessary
witnesses and focused on issues, such as her eldest daughter’s shooting, which
were neither relevant nor necessary.

[
66
]

I agree with Mr. Friedlander that he called
these witnesses in order to address a number of the unfounded allegations which
Ms. Claman brought against him and his parenting abilities.

[
67
]

Third, Ms. Claman submits that the relative
financial circumstances of the parties, as well as the significant hardship
such an award would place upon her, militate against an award of special costs.
She claims that she is faced with significant debt and financial
responsibilities and attached an updated F8 financial statement filed October
31, 2014, more than three months after the trial was completed, to her costs
submissions.

[
68
]

Mr. Friedlander objects to the admissions of Ms. Claman’s
new F8 financial statement on the basis that costs are to be assessed based on
the circumstances at the time of trial:
Rockwell v. Rockwell
,
[1999]
B.C.J. No. 2238 at para. 8 (S.C.)
. He further asserts that this updated
financial statement should not be believed any more than the one on which Ms. Claman
was cross-examined at trial. He submits that if Ms. Claman’s new financial
statement is admitted, then his affidavit sworn on January 22, 2015 in response
to the stay application should also be reviewed by the court as evidence
related to Ms. Claman’s current lifestyle and new business ventures.

[
69
]

I do not find that Ms. Claman has a
legitimate hardship claim. I have already drawn an adverse inference that Ms. Claman
is probably concealing assets at para. 21 of my November Reasons. I was
unable to rely on Ms. Claman’s evidence related to her assets and debts
and she failed to provide the necessary documentation to enable a valuation to proceed
in respect of her business interests. It would be incredulous to allow her to
now claim hardship after these findings which, in large part, are the basis for
the award for special costs.

[
70
]

In light of my findings regarding Ms. Claman’s
non-disclosure, I do not find that an award of special costs would upset the
balance of the court’s orders in this proceeding.

IV.

conclusion

[
71
]

Mr. Friedlander is awarded special costs of the
case.

[
72
]

I refer this matter to the registrar to
determine the amount of special costs.

[
73
]

It is unnecessary to consider the alternative
costs submissions of the parties.

“Gropper J.”
